source.what: Joby Aviation site header (careers page) — the fixed navigation bar and its menu overlay, distilled for structure, layout, typography and motion. Scoped to the nav only; the rest of the page is not graded.
source.method: Chromium (ms-playwright chromium-1234) driven by puppeteer-core, one isolated browser context per width and per state. Three viewports: 1440x900, 834x1112, 390x844 (deviceScaleFactor 1). Four states captured per viewport: default at page top, scrolled down 1400px, scrolled back up to 1150px (pill state), and menu open after a synthetic click on the menu opener. Every number below comes from getComputedStyle (including ::before pseudo-element styles), getBoundingClientRect, resolved CSS custom properties on :root, and the authored CSS rules read out of the document stylesheets, plus document.getAnimations() sampled every 90ms from the first frame after the click. Discrete scroll travel was used (0 -> 1400 -> 1150) with 1.1-1.8s settles so each state was fully reached before measurement.
gaps: The scroll-driven hide/show threshold is not fully characterised. Measured: topNav translateY is 6px at scrollY 0 and 0.72px mid-entrance, -84px (fully retracted) at scrollY 200 and beyond, and 6px again once scrolled up from 1500 to 1200. A single 200px-down step produced full retraction, so the exact trigger point between 0 and 200px was not isolated, and no velocity dependence was tested.

The reveal transition (.4s) and the retract transition (.5s) were sampled but their easing curves were read from authored CSS rather than measured frame by frame; no intermediate transform samples were captured for the hide/show pair.
The close animation (menu shutting) was not captured; only the opening sequence was sampled.
Focus-visible states, keyboard traversal order, and screen-reader announcement of the panel were not captured.
Reduced-motion behaviour was not tested; no prefers-reduced-motion branch was confirmed in the authored rules.
The nav's behaviour over a page with a light hero was not captured. The careers hero is orange, which selects the hero state variant (white menu lines); the hero-dark variant was not exercised.
The tablet viewport in this capture is 834x1112 (portrait), matching the project's standard capture matrix, not an iPad-native landscape.
source.notes: The header has four distinct states, and they are genuinely four, not two. (1) DEFAULT: no surface at all — the bar is transparent and its contents sit directly on the hero. (2) RETRACTED: scrolled down, the whole bar translates up and off, leaving no header. (3) PILL: scrolled back up, a cream rounded slab fades in behind the bar, floating inset from the page edge. (4) OPEN: the bar stays, a full-width colour panel unrolls beneath it in layered bands, and the bar's own content restyles to sit on that panel. The state machine is the design. Everything below is measured.

element_inventory.note: 80px tall at 1440, 8rem; carries the pill as a ::before
the cream rounded slab; not an element, a pseudo-element
full-viewport dark layer shown behind the open panel at 60% opacity
the colour slab that unrolls; four stacked layers retract in sequence
33x33px, two 2px bars that cross into a close glyph
the page name beside the opener; slides out and fades on open
centred mark, 51x32px at 1440; slides and reveals wordmark on open
'Investors' with arrow; swaps label on hover via an in/out pair
16-column grid, same 16px gutter as the page
three lists: main, sub, social, each with its own stagger

parts.name: Four-state header
parts.description: The header is a state machine with four distinct appearances, each reached by a different trigger: transparent over the hero at page top, fully retracted while scrolling down, a floating cream pill when scrolling back up, and an open colour panel when the menu is activated. No state is a variation of another — the surface, the bar's own styling and the content all change together.
parts.entry_test: Give the header one permanent background and it stops being this header. The four-state cycle IS the identity; a static bar with a menu would fail the removal test immediately.
parts.recipe: Implement as four class states on the nav root, mutually exclusive except where noted: no class (default), .navHidden (scrolled down), .hero / .hero-dark (over a hero, suppresses the pill and switches bar content to white), .open (menu open). Drive default/retracted/pill from a scroll-direction listener that toggles .navHidden on downward scroll and clears it on upward scroll; drive .hero from the page template. Measurements: bar translateY is 6px at rest (the design sits the bar 0.6rem low), -84px when retracted, 6px again in the pill state. The bar height is 8rem (80px at the 1440 root of 10px). Never let two surface states paint at once: the authored rules explicitly cancel the pill on .hero and on .open.

checks.check: Four distinct header states exist and are reachable: default transparent, retracted, pill, open
Default state paints no background on the bar or the nav root
Retracted state translates the bar fully out of view (about -105% of bar height)
Pill state and open state never paint simultaneously
Bar rest offset is a small non-zero step (6px at 1440), not exactly 0

evidence: default: topNav transform matrix(1,0,0,1,0,0.72) mid-settle and matrix(1,0,0,1,0,6) settled; nav root background rgba(0,0,0,0); bar background rgba(0,0,0,0)
retracted: topNav transform matrix(1,0,0,1,0,-84) at scrollY 200 through 1500; authored rule .navHidden .topNav { transform: translateY(-100%) }
pill: topNav transform matrix(1,0,0,1,0,6) with topNav::before opacity 1
open: nav root class list reads 'nav hero open animateIn'
authored: .open .topNav::before { opacity: 0 } and .hero .topNav::before { opacity: 0 }

parts.name: Hide on down, return on up
parts.description: Scrolling down retracts the bar entirely so the viewport is clean; scrolling up brings it back with the pill surface. The two directions get different durations — the retract is slower than the reveal — so the bar leaves deliberately and returns promptly.
parts.entry_test: Make the bar permanently fixed and the page loses its whole scroll rhythm; make it disappear without a different return treatment and the reappearance reads as a glitch rather than a state.
parts.recipe: Toggle .navHidden on downward scroll past a small threshold and remove it on any upward scroll. Retract: transform .5s cubic-bezier(.32,0,.67,0) — an ease-in, so it accelerates away. Reveal: transform .4s cubic-bezier(.33,1,.68,1) — an ease-out-cubic, so it arrives quickly and settles. The asymmetry is the point: 500ms out, 400ms back, different curves. Measured travel is 0 to -84px, i.e. -105% of the 80px bar height.

checks.check: Scrolling down retracts the bar fully out of the viewport
Scrolling up restores the bar with the pill surface, not the transparent default
Retract and reveal use different durations (500ms vs 400ms observed)
Retract uses an ease-in and reveal uses an ease-out, so the curves differ in direction
The bar returns on the first upward travel rather than only at the page top

evidence: authored: .topNav { transition: transform .4s var(--ease-out-cubic) } with --ease-out-cubic = cubic-bezier(.33,1,.68,1)
authored: .navHidden .topNav { transform: translateY(-100%) } and .topNav.navHidden { transition: transform .5s var(--ease-in-cubic) } with --ease-in-cubic = cubic-bezier(.32,0,.67,0)
measured: retracted at scrollY 200, 500, 900, 1200, 1500; restored to translateY(6px) at scrollY 1200, 900, 600, 300, 100, 0 after the upward pass
travel: 0 to -84px on an 80px bar = -105%

parts.name: The floating pill
parts.description: The return surface is a cream slab with fully rounded ends that spans the page inside its own inset, floating clear of the viewport edges — it is a pill, not a full-width bar. It is drawn as a pseudo-element behind the bar's content, so the content does not move when the surface appears and the bar can carry a different surface in other states without touching layout.
parts.entry_test: Widen the slab to the viewport edges and the bar becomes a conventional sticky header; the inset rounded slab floating over content is what makes the reappearance feel like an object rather than a banner.
parts.recipe: Draw the surface as topNav::before, absolutely positioned inside the bar: top 1rem, left 2.4rem, width calc(100% - 4.8rem), height 6rem, background the cream token #F5F4DF, border-radius 56px, box-shadow rgba(0,0,0,0.23) 0 1px 1px, z-index -1. Inset is therefore 24px horizontally and 10px vertically at the 1440 root, and the slab is 60px tall inside an 80px bar. Fade it, do not slide it: opacity .3s ease-out-cubic with an 800ms delay when leaving the hero, and .4s with no delay when leaving the open state. Measurements: 1440 slab is 1392x60 at x24 y10; 834 slab is 794.9x48.9 at x19.5 y8.1; 390 slab is 373.4x47.8 at x8.3 y0.

checks.check: The surface is a rounded slab inset from both viewport edges, not full-bleed
Corner radius is fully rounded relative to slab height (56px on a 60px slab)
Surface is a pseudo-element or background layer behind the content, so content geometry is unchanged between states
Inset scales with the root: 24px/10px at 1440, 19.5px/8.1px at 834, 8.3px/0 at 390
A single soft shadow, about 1px offset and low opacity, sits under the slab

parts.name: Layered panel unroll
parts.description: Opening the menu does not fade a panel in. A full-width colour slab unrolls downward from behind the bar, and behind it four stacked colour bands — pink, orange, blue, dark blue, at 50/70/100/100% heights — retract upward in sequence (scaleY to 0) with staggered timing. The overlapping travel of the slab and the bands is what produces the accordion feel; the colours are glimpsed as the bands collapse.
parts.entry_test: Replace the layered unroll with a simple fade and the menu becomes an ordinary overlay; the sequenced colour bands sliding against each other are the gesture that makes this menu recognisable.
parts.recipe: Stack inside the nav, absolutely positioned, all starting at translateY(-100%) with height calc(100% + 1.2rem) so a 1.2rem lip stays hidden above. Open: set the slab and overlay to translateY(0) with transform .7s cubic-bezier(.65,0,.35,1) (in-out-cubic) and no delay; set each overlayLayer to scaleY(0) with transformOrigin center bottom, at .88s / 1.01s / .75s delay .32s / .75s delay .45s for layers 1-4. Because the layers sit at z-index 4/3/2/1 and the slab at z-index 2, the bands peel away upward as the slab arrives. Layer heights and colours: layer 1 pink #FFD9C9 at 50%, layer 2 orange #EB6110 at 70%, layer 3 blue #007AE5 at 100%, layer 4 dark blue #1C3F99 at 100%. Reversed durations on close are authored separately (.73s / .9s / .63s / .52s with delays .25s / .105s / .105s / 0).

checks.check: Panel opens by expanding from behind the bar, not by fading in place
At least three stacked colour layers retract in sequence with distinct delays
Layers use scaleY with transform-origin at bottom, so they peel upward
Layer heights differ (50% / 70% / 100% / 100% observed)
Panel expands over about 700ms with an in-out curve

parts.name: Opener morphs to close
parts.description: The menu control is two thin bars that cross into a close glyph. The same button rotates its own lines 45 degrees in opposite directions and re-colours them from black to white as the panel's blue surface arrives behind it, while the current-page label slides out to the right and fades, and the close label fades in.
parts.entry_test: Swap the morph for an icon replacement and the control stops being part of the motion language; the bars crossing in place is what ties the button to the panel it opens.
parts.recipe: Build the control as a 3.3rem square button with two absolutely positioned pseudo-element bars, each 3.3rem wide, 2px tall, border-radius 100px, at top calc(50% - 2.5px) and calc(50% + 2.5px), both centred with translate(-50%,-50%). Open state: both bars take width 100%, the first moves translateY(2.5px) and the second translateY(-2.5px) so they meet on the centre line, then each rotates 45 degrees in opposite directions; bars animate transform .7s cubic-bezier(.65,0,.35,1). Colour changes black to white over .4s ease-out-cubic, with the width change on a .3s delay. The button itself translates -1.6rem left so the pair stays optically centred against the incoming label. The current-page label leaves with transform .4s in-out-cubic translate(2rem) plus opacity 0, and the close label arrives on a 200ms delay.

checks.check: Open control is two bars rotated into a cross, in the same button position
Bar colour flips to the colour that reads against the open panel
Current-page label fades out and slides as the panel opens
Bar rotation runs about 700ms on an in-out curve
Two bars animate at the same duration so the cross forms symmetrically

parts.name: Staggered link arrival
parts.description: The panel's link lists do not appear together. Each link rises from below (translateY) while fading in, and the three lists are staggered against each other — the main links come up first and fast, the sub-links and social links follow much later on a long, slow, decelerating curve.
parts.entry_test: Land every link at once and the panel loses its unrolling feel; the stagger is what makes the panel read as still settling after the surface has arrived.
parts.recipe: Seed the links below and invisible, then clear on open. Main links: li at transform translateY(4rem), opacity 0, cleared with opacity 50ms cubic-bezier(.32,0,.67,0) and transform 667ms cubic-bezier(.2,.21,0,1); the per-item delay steps by 83ms (820, 903, 986, 1069, 1152ms measured). Sub links: li at translateY(1rem), cleared with opacity .4s in-out-cubic and transform 2.4s cubic-bezier(.16,1,.3,1), delay starting 800ms and stepping 100ms. Social links: li at translateY(1.5rem), same 2.4s curve and 100ms steps. The long 2.4s transform on the lower lists is deliberate: it lingers so the panel appears to keep opening after the colour surface has stopped. Never give the three lists the same duration or the same delay base.

checks.check: Panel links animate in individually rather than appearing with the panel
Main links use a faster curve and shorter duration than the sub/social lists
Per-item delay steps are uniform within a list (83ms for main, 100ms for sub/social observed)
Links rise from below via translateY, not a fade alone
The lowest list still uses a decelerating ease-out-expo curve

parts.name: Bar content restyles per state
parts.description: The bar's own contents change colour and position by state so they always read against whatever surface is behind them: dark on the cream pill, dark on the orange hero with white opener bars, white on the blue open panel. The current-page label and the opener are the elements that move; the logo shifts aside to reveal the wordmark when the panel is open.
parts.entry_test: Keep one content treatment across all four states and the bar becomes illegible on at least two of them; the per-state restyling is what lets one bar live on four surfaces.
parts.recipe: Tie content colour to the state class, not to a media query. On hero templates the default state paints the opener bars with the white token and widens the left group gap to 4.6rem. In the open state the current-page label slides out entirely and the logo slides -4.6rem left while its wordmark fades in and its SVG slides from translate(-100%) to 0 over .5s cubic-bezier(.2,.21,0,1), revealing 'Joby'. In the pill state the content is dark on cream. The bar itself never changes height between default, pill and open — only the surface and the content change.

checks.check: Bar content colour differs per surface so it stays legible in all four states
Current-page label is removed from the bar when the panel is open
Logo reveals its wordmark on open by sliding the mark aside and unmasking the text
Bar height is unchanged between default, pill and open states
Hero templates use a distinct content treatment from the plain default (white opener bars)

parts.name: Panel sits on the page grid
parts.description: The open panel's contents are laid out on the same 16-column grid with the same gutter and base padding as the rest of the page, so the menu is a page surface rather than a bespoke overlay. Panel padding is fluid — expressed against viewport height — so the panel grows with short and tall viewports alike.
parts.entry_test: Lay the panel out free-form and it stops reading as part of the site; sharing the page's grid and padding is what makes the overlay feel like a room in the same building.
parts.recipe: navOpen is display grid with grid-template-columns repeat(var(--grid-columns), 1fr) and column-gap var(--gutter-width), padding 0 var(--base-padding); with --grid-columns 16, --gutter-width 1.6rem and --base-padding 4rem those resolve to a 16-track grid, 16px gutter and 40px side padding at a 10px root. Vertical padding is fluid: min(16rem, 17.7vh) var(--base-padding) 8rem. At 390 the tokens change only in base padding (1.6rem, i.e. 16.64px) while the column count and gutter token hold. Panel height is content-driven (fit-content) — 560.6px at 1440, 457.2px at 834, 773.3px at 390 — and is NOT a fixed viewport fraction at desktop; only the mobile viewport is effectively filled.

checks.check: Panel uses the same column count as the page (16) and its gutter token
Panel side padding uses the shared base-padding token, not a bespoke value
Panel top padding is fluid against viewport height, capped at a rem maximum
Panel height is content-driven, not a hard-coded fraction of the viewport
Column count and gutter tokens are shared with the page rather than redeclared

parts.name: Fluid rem root
parts.description: The whole header — bar height, pill inset, radius, control sizes, type — is authored in rem against a root font-size that itself scales with the viewport. At 1440 the root is 10px, at 834 it is 8.14px, at 390 it is 10.4px. Everything therefore shrinks and grows as one system without a single media-query override for the header's internals.
parts.entry_test: Pin the root at 16px and every nav value needs its own breakpoint; the fluid root is what makes the whole header collapse proportionally.
parts.recipe: Set the html font-size fluidly (a vw-derived value with clamps) and author the header exclusively in rem. Measured roots: 10px at 1440w, 8.14453px at 834w, 10.4px at 390w. Bar height 8rem therefore renders 80px / 65.2px / 83.2px; the pill inset 2.4rem renders 24px / 19.5px / 25px; the opener 3.3rem renders 33px / 26.9px / 34.3px. Note the root is not monotonic with width — it dips at 834 and rises at 390 — because the middle tier scales the root down while the mobile tier raises it again; preserve that shape rather than replacing it with a monotonic ramp.

checks.check: Header dimensions are authored in rem, not px
Root font-size varies with viewport (10px / 8.14px / 10.4px observed)
Bar height, pill inset and control sizes all scale together with the root
No per-breakpoint override is needed for header internals
Border-radius is authored in px (56px) so the pill stays fully rounded at every root size

parts.name: A named easing library
parts.description: Every motion in the header draws from a small named set of custom-property easings rather than ad-hoc cubic-beziers: an in-out cubic for surfaces, an out-cubic for arriving content, an ease-in for departing content, an out-expo for the long link settle, a snappy for the fast link rise, and a back curve used once for the opener. Durations cluster at 300-400ms for controls and 520-1010ms for the panel.
parts.entry_test: Replace the named set with per-rule beziers and the header's motion stops being one language; the shared vocabulary is what makes four different animations read as one system.
parts.recipe: Declare the easing set once on :root and reference it by name everywhere: --ease-in-out-cubic cubic-bezier(.65,0,.35,1) for surfaces and panel travel; --ease-out-cubic cubic-bezier(.33,1,.68,1) for content arriving; --ease-in-cubic cubic-bezier(.32,0,.67,0) for content leaving; --ease-out-expo cubic-bezier(.16,1,.3,1) for the long link settle; --ease-snappy cubic-bezier(.2,.21,0,1) for the fast link rise; --ease-in-out-back cubic-bezier(.68,-.6,.32,1.6) reserved for the opener; --ease-out-curve-cubic cubic-bezier(.35,.2,0,1). Keep control durations in a 200-400ms band and panel durations in a 500-1010ms band; nothing in the header runs longer than about 2.4s, and that exception is the deliberate linger on the lowest link list.

checks.check: Easings are declared as named custom properties and referenced, not repeated inline
At least four distinct named curves are in use across surfaces, arrivals and departures
Surfaces use an in-out curve; arriving content uses an ease-out; departing content uses an ease-in
Control transitions sit in a 200-400ms band and panel transitions in a 500-1010ms band
The overshoot back-curve is used sparingly (one control), not across the panel

limitations: The scroll threshold that triggers retraction was not isolated. A 200px downward step produced full retraction (translateY -84px); the exact point between 0 and 200px, and any velocity dependence, is unknown. The direction rule itself is confirmed: retract on down, restore on up.

No intermediate frames were sampled for the retract/reveal pair. Their durations and curves are read from authored CSS (.5s ease-in-cubic out, .4s ease-out-cubic back) rather than measured from transform samples.
The close sequence was not captured; only the opening animation was sampled (35 concurrent animations, sampled every 90ms from 9ms after the click).

The open-state link font sizes reported here (16px per li at 1440) conflict with the rendered 64px on the link spans themselves: the li elements carry an inherited 16px while their child spans render at 64px/500. The type values above record the rendered span sizes, which are what a viewer sees; the li-level 16px is a cascade artifact of this implementation and is not treated as the design intent.

Panel type sizes are reported at the 1440 fixed tier. The panel scales with the fluid root at 834 (13.03px li-level) and 390 (16.64px), but the rendered span sizes at those widths were not separately resolved, so the true mobile display size is inferred from the root factor rather than measured directly.

The 390 mobile panel renders 773.3px tall in an 844px viewport (92% of viewport height) and the nav element itself measures 821px; the panel is content-driven and happens to nearly fill a small viewport rather than being authored as a fixed full-height surface. Whether it is intended to fill exactly on shorter devices was not tested.
Focus, keyboard traversal, reduced-motion behaviour and screen-reader announcement of the panel state were not captured.

Only the careers template was captured. The hero state variant (white opener bars, suppressed pill) was exercised because careers has an orange hero; the hero-dark variant and the technologyNav variant that hides the current-page label were read from authored CSS but not exercised on a live page.
Nav dropdown behaviour (.dropwdownOpen, which shows the scrim at 0.4 instead of 0.6) was read from CSS but not exercised.
